title: If Christ be not risen (1 Corinthians 15:14; CCC 639)
hookLine: Catholics hold the resurrection happened, not as a metaphor

lines: SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.
HE BETS EVERYTHING ON ONE EVENT.
cards: Word reaches the man who founded the church in Corinth: some members are saying the dead don't really rise. He could soften it. Say the story is beautiful, whatever happened.

Say what matters is what Jesus taught. Instead he writes one of the bluntest sentences you could put in a letter: if it didn't happen, our preaching is empty, and so is your faith. He bets everything on one event.
The writer is Paul, the letter is First Corinthians, and the Catholic Church still stands behind his bet.

teach.h: IF NOT, OUR FAITH IS VAIN.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "And if Christ be not risen again, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." Vain means empty.
Paul goes further: if Christ isn't raised, Christians are still in their sins, and if their hope is for this life only, they are of all people the most miserable. Then the witnesses.

teach.h: MORE THAN FIVE HUNDRED AT ONCE.
teach.b: Just before this, Paul lists who saw the risen Jesus: Cephas, that's Peter, then the apostles, then more than five hundred people at once, many of whom, he says, are still alive.
That detail reads like an invitation: go and ask them. And Paul says he is handing on what he himself received, so the list was already being passed along before he wrote it down.

teach.h: A REAL EVENT, NOT A METAPHOR.
teach.b: The Catechism calls the resurrection a real event, with manifestations that were historically witnessed, as the New Testament shows. Not a metaphor for the disciples' hope, not a way of saying his teaching lived on.

The tomb was empty, and he was seen. And the Catechism points out that the disciples were not easy believers: they thought the women's report was nonsense, and Thomas refused to believe unless he could touch the wounds.
Not a return to the old life, the way Lazarus came back and would later die again.
Catholics say Jesus rose into a glorified life that death can't touch: still bearing the wounds, able to eat with friends, no longer bound by locked doors.
And in Matthew, the angel at the empty tomb answers Paul's if in three words: he is risen.

how: Catholics profess every Sunday in the Creed that Christ rose on the third day, celebrate the resurrection for the fifty days of Easter, and in many communities, especially Eastern Catholic ones, greet each other at Easter with Christ is risen, and the reply, he is truly risen.

o: a hymn sung by the women on Easter morning
he was raised: the angel's word at the empty tomb
the stone rolled back from the tomb's door

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Catholic teaching treats the resurrection as a metaphor for the disciples' hope
the Catechism calls it a real event: the tomb was empty and he was seen.
Paul says that if Christ is not risen, faith is vain
"then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain."
Jesus rose the way Lazarus did, back to his old life
Catholics say he rose into a glorified life death can't touch, still bearing his wounds.

games.q: you're Paul. some in Corinth say the dead don't rise. how do you answer them?
o: say the story is beautiful whatever happened.
say that if Christ isn't risen, the faith is empty.
say it doesn't really matter either way.
games.why: Paul bets everything: if Christ be not risen, preaching and faith are vain. then he lists the witnesses.

practice: Picture the early morning: the stone rolled back, the women running, Peter running after them.
Then say the three words quietly, he is risen, and again, slower, and notice what comes, joy, doubt or both, and let it be honest; Thomas had doubt, and he's a saint.
If you pray, you can bring the doubt and the joy to God together.

wordCard.voice: Egerthe, the Greek word the angel uses at the empty tomb: he was raised, he is risen. Paul's whole bet on one event.
